TRANSCRIPT OF PROCEEDINGS
ROYAL COMMISSION ON ANTISEMITISM
AND SOCIAL COHESION
WEDNESDAY, 29 JULY 2026
AT 10:00AM (AEST)
HEARING BLOCK 6, DAY 2
THE HONOURABLE VIRGINIA BELL AC SC,
COMMISSIONER
MR RICHARD LANCASTER SC
MS TAMARA PHILLIPS

<THE HEARING RESUMED AT 10.00 AM
COMMISSIONER: Yes, Ms Phillips.
MS PHILLIPS: Commissioner, the first witnesses this morning will be giving
evidence concurrently. They are Dr Adam Gordon and Dr Jack Green but I should
also indicate that they are represented and there are some other appearances from
other witnesses who will be giving evidence today.
COMMISSIONER: Yes.
MS CONSTABLE: Commissioner, I appear for Dr Jack Green and Dr Adam
Gordon. S.M. Constable, C-o-n-s-t-a-b-l-e.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you. And - yes?
MS CAIRNS: Commissioner, Ms Cairns, C-a-i-r-n-s. I appear for Dr Dai, D-a-i.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. Very well. Thank you, Ms Cairns. Otherwise the
appearances are - no?
MR JELLIS SC: Yes. Good morning, Commissioner. My name is Ben Jellis. I
appear with Tamir Katz, with your leave, for Justin Untersteiner of AHPRA.
COMMISSIONER: Yes, indeed, you have that leave. Yes.
MS PHILLIPS: Could the doctors please come forward.
<ADAM GORDON, AFFIRMED
<JACK GREEN, AFFIRMED
COMMISSIONER: Yes, Doctors, do take your seat. Is there some reason we are
taking the evidence conjointly?
MS PHILLIPS: Commissioner, they're two representatives of the same organisation
with different perspectives.
COMMISSIONER: Yes.
MS PHILLIPS: Dr Green, can I ask you to state your full name, please?
DR GREEN: Jack Green.
MS PHILLIPS: You have prepared a witness statement that is dated 28 July 2026?
DR GREEN: Yes.

MS PHILLIPS: Are the contents of that statement true and correct to the best of
your knowledge and belief?
DR GREEN: It is.
MS PHILLIPS: Commissioner, I tender that witness statement. It has Doc ID
STAT.8999.0001.0603_R.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. Dr Green's statement will be admitted as an exhibit.
MS PHILLIPS: And, Dr Gordon, can you please state your full name.
DR GORDON: Adam Gordon.
MR LANCASTER SC: You have prepared a witness statement that is dated 28 July
2026?
DR GORDON: I have.
MS PHILLIPS: Is the content of that statement true and correct to the best of your
knowledge and belief?
DR GORDON: That is true.
MS PHILLIPS: I tender that statement, Commissioner. It has Doc ID
STAT.8999.0001.0594_R.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. Dr Gordon's statement will also be received as an exhibit.
MS PHILLIPS: Dr Green, can I start with you. You were raised in Melbourne's
Jewish community; is that right?
DR GREEN: Yes, I was.
MS PHILLIPS: And both of your parents were Holocaust survivors who lost most
of their families in that event and came to Australia as refugees?
DR GREEN: Yes. Yes, they did.
MS PHILLIPS: You are a volunteer guide at the Melbourne Holocaust Museum,
and that has shaped a lot of your perspective about Jewish history; is that right?
DR GREEN: Yes, it has.
MS PHILLIPS: And you are also a qualified, a qualified dermatologist?

DR GREEN: I am.
MS PHILLIPS: And general practitioner?
DR GREEN: I have both qualifications, yes.
MS PHILLIPS: And is it right that you have a private practice and that you also
maintain public appointments at various hospitals as a consultant dermatologist?
DR GREEN: Yes, I do.
MS PHILLIPS: You've commenced your witness statement by noting that, in your
own professional practice, you do not display or wear political symbols and that you
do not initiate political discussions with your own patients, and that your experience
is that this approach works. Would you like to comment on that?
DR GREEN: Yes. So as a dermatologist I have a particular interest in skin of colour
dermatology. So a lot of the patients I see are from a different background to mine.
Quite a diverse population. Many of them have been refugees themselves from
various parts of the world. And in my own practice, seeing this varied population,
I do not discuss politics. I think that cultural sensitivity is very important and,
basically, the patients are there to be treated. I am their doctor and that is the most
important thing. It's a trust relationship, and there is no place for politicisation in
health practice. And that's the way I have been practising for a long time, and I've
never had any problems, and it's worked for me and it's worked for my patients.
MS PHILLIPS: And, Dr Green, by reference to paragraph 9 of your witness
statement, are you able to tell me about the Australasian Jewish Medical Federation
and your own role in that organisation?
DR GREEN: Yes. I've been the President since 2019. The organisation was an
amalgamation of medical organisations both in Victoria and New South Wales, and
the origins are different and quite interesting. So, refugee medical practitioners who
came here in the 1930s from Nazi Germany, from Austria and then after the
Holocaust from other areas wanted to re-establish themselves, and if they were to
retrain in Victoria, they needed to go back to medical school for five years. In New
South Wales, it was three years. They flocked to New South Wales, and they faced
a lot of difficulties and pressures retraining. And so they formed their own self-help
group, New South Wales Jewish Doctors Society, in the 1950s.
In Victoria, there were more locally trained doctors and after the creation of the State
of Israel, they created an Australian affiliate of the Israel Medical Association, also
in the 1950s. Then in the 1980s, the two organisations amalgamated into the
Australasian Jewish Medical Federation.

MS PHILLIPS: You have said that in your involvement with the organisation, the
AJMF, prior to the 7th October 2023, the organisation hardly ever received reports of
antisemitism within healthcare?
DR GREEN: That is correct. I only ever dealt with one minor incident, and the
organisation was past its heyday and there was a lot less activity than had been in
earlier decades. It did become busy during the COVID years, so 2020 to 2022, I'd set
up a WhatsApp group and there was a lot of discussion about the pressures of
practice and issues to do with the pandemic. It was very busy, but there wasn't
a discussion of antisemitism in that WhatsApp group. It just really wasn't there. Even
though it was quite busy.
MS PHILLIPS: Can you comment on how things changed for the organisation after
the 7th of October 2023?
DR GREEN: So after the 7th of October, I restarted the WhatsApp group and this
time a lot of people joined very quickly. It peaked at 450 individuals on that group.
And what we were seeing were people were talking about lots of examples of
antisemitism in the health sector. There was increased politicisation in the health
sector. There was a lot of social media postings, and it was - there was a lot of
increasingly stressed Jewish medical practitioners, and they started contacting us,
telling us some of these stories and there was increasing need for advocacy.
MS PHILLIPS: Dr Gordon, I might come to you at this point. Is it right you were
yourself raised in a traditional Jewish home in Melbourne?
DR GORDON: Correct.
MS PHILLIPS: And are you a medical professional with a specialisation in
gastroenterology.
DR GORDON: Correct.
MS PHILLIPS: And you currently work in the private healthcare sector, but
previously, for over 20 years, you worked within the public healthcare system in
Victoria?
DR GORDON: Correct.
MS PHILLIPS: And you completed your medical training at the Alfred Hospital.
DR GORDON: Correct.
MS PHILLIPS: And you’ve said in your witness statement - this is at paragraph 6 -
that you had never experienced antisemitism in Melbourne before the 7th of October
2023?

DR GORDON: Correct.
MS PHILLIPS: And you have noted in your statement - this is at paragraph 9 - that
after the 7th of October you established a dedicated advocacy committee which you
have said was to provide support to Jewish doctors and healthcare workers who had
experienced antisemitism?
DR GORDON: Correct.
MS PHILLIPS: And is it right that you then brought that committee into the AJMF
as a subcommittee within the Victorian branch of that organisation?
DR GORDON: Correct.
MS PHILLIPS: And is it the case that you subsequently served as Vice President of
the Victorian branch of the AJMF from about February of 2024 until December of
2025?
DR GORDON: Correct.
MS PHILLIPS: Are you able to indicate why it was that you saw the need to
establish the advocacy committee that you’ve described?
DR GORDON: So I was a member of the WhatsApp group that Jack spoke to and
set up. And there were a lot of doctors expressing that they'd been marginalised,
isolated professionally, experiencing antisemitism and so there was a lot of despair
on the WhatsApp group. And people were giving support to these people who have
been having these experiences. But in terms of practicality, a lot of these doctors who
had been facing the system by themselves weren't achieving fair outcomes. And
there were also doctors and other healthcare professionals who were experiencing
antisemitism who were fearful of approaching management because of impact on
their job, on their career - particularly junior medical staff who were in a very
vulnerable position in the hierarchy in the public healthcare system.
And so I felt that if there was a group that could speak for these people, we would be
able to get further than the individuals speaking for themselves who weren't,
unfortunately, getting very far.
MS PHILLIPS: And, Dr Gordon, can I take you to paragraph 17 of your witness
statement. You've noted there that you have observed through your role in the AJMF
that there has been a pervasive sense of loss of safety or loss of safety in the
workplace and in professional networks amongst Jewish medical professionals and
a fear of displaying Jewish identity. Are you able to comment on how you have seen
that arise and the kinds of behaviour changes amongst Jewish medical professionals
that can accompany that sense of loss of safety?

DR GORDON: Well, doctors are afraid to display symbols indicating they are
Jewish. So a lot of people have, you know, Magen David or Star of David that they
might wear on a chain, and people either conceal those kinds of things or don't wear
them at all. They definitely don't broach topics about being Jewish in group settings
at work, because that's an invitation for, you know, discussion, confrontation about
conflict and Jewish identity, and people are afraid.
MS PHILLIPS: Dr Green, can I come to you, please. In your witness statement,
from paragraph 18, you've outlined several themes under a heading which reads
Incidents Involving Patients and Healthcare Workers. And the first topic that you
address under that heading refers to media reports in February 2025 that healthcare
workers were filmed making comments about refusing to treat Israeli patients. And
I'm not going to ask you about the specifics of that incident, but can I ask you, by
reference to paragraph 20 of your witness statement, what Jewish healthcare
professionals shared with you about the impact of some of those reports on them and
their circles.
DR GREEN: Well, what was discussed was concern about trust in the healthcare
system, both for medical practitioners and Jewish patients, and the concern that there
would be some risk that they might not be treated equally and fairly in the health
system. And we need trust in our health system for the health of that health system,
and if there's - if that's affected, if that's fractured, that's a really unfortunate
situation, and this is what was being expressed.
MS PHILLIPS: And you've described at paragraph 21 of your witness statement
a report that was made to the AJMF by a community paediatrician. Can you describe
that report?
DR GREEN: I might read that:
"A community paediatrician reported to AJMF that the father of a child he was
consulting with, who did not know the doctor was Jewish, had told him that he had
terminated the services of a National Disability Insurance Scheme coordinator upon
learning that the coordinator was Jewish. The father is reported to have stated that
he would ‘never trust a Jew to manage his money.’"
And this is an old trope, a Jewish trope, and it's unfortunate that we're seeing it here
in the health system.
MS PHILLIPS: And another incident that you have referred to is at paragraph 30 of
your witness statement, the hospital incident in the Northern Territory that AJMF
became aware of that occurred in August 2025. What did your organisation learn
about that incident?
DR GREEN: So that was an incident in which the obstetrician was wearing
a political symbol, a keffiyeh-themed lanyard displaying a Palestinian flag, and the

patient and the patient's partner were Australians, one of them was Israeli-born, and
I'll just read this out:
"Observing overt political symbols associated with the current conflict in which their
family and friends have been affected worn by their treating doctor caused the
patient significant distress and raised immediate concerns about whether they would
receive impartial and equitable care.
And as reported to the AJMF, the patient attempted to raise her concerns directly
with the obstetrician, but her concerns were not acknowledged, and this left the
patient feeling excluded and unsafe in the doctor's care.”
Now, if it was - had been at that time unacceptable for that medical practitioner to
wear a political symbol, then we would never have got into this problem where
that - the patient would be feeling unsafe. It really fractures the doctor/patient
relationship.
And healthcare - that's just a negative for healthcare. And so if there were would
have been regulations at that time, and a culture of not allowing the wearing of those
political symbols, then this would have been prevented. It seems pretty clear.
MS PHILLIPS: And, Dr Green, can I take you to paragraph 35 of your statement.
You have given an example there, I think, of an instance where some of the
boundaries that you've just been referring to about politicisation in the clinical
environment were enforced to a constructive outcome. Can you explain what
happened in that instance?
DR GREEN: So in this situation, it was a junior medical resident and someone in
the team spoke to the senior clinician in charge. It was all done quietly to say
well - and by this time, there had already been a directive from the Victorian
government - this occurred in Victoria - that political symbols should not be worn.
The senior doctor had a quiet word with the junior doctor and that was the end of the
matter. And it was dealt with very well, and it didn't have to be out in public. And if
matters can be resolved in a non-confrontational way, I'm all for that.
MS PHILLIPS: And, Dr Green, if I can take you to paragraph 28 of your statement,
you've said that, from your perspective, social media presents a particularly difficult
challenge because it occupies a grey zone between personal expression and
professional identity. Are you able to articulate what you have in mind by that grey
zone?
DR GREEN: Well, people have a right to political expression. People have - of
course have a right to express themselves. But, as medical practitioners, to maintain
trust in our system - not just medical practitioners, all health practitioners - there are
restrictions compared to other work environments because of that trust, of that power
differential between the medical practitioner and the patient. And we need to make
sure that that trust is maintained in the system.

I could give a little bit of a parallel. In the legal system, there are also restrictions on
legal practitioners or judges making public comments, because you don't want
someone coming up in front of a judge and that judge has a particular partisan view,
and they might not feel that it is fair. So there's some sort of parallel with that. And
the other thing is that I think there's a difference in social media whether someone
identifies themselves as a medical practitioner and where they're from, and if they
don't. So I think there needs to be caution - caution about it.
MS PHILLIPS: Dr Gordon, can I ask you, like Dr Green, in your own witness
statement, you have expressed some concerns surrounding the politicisation of
healthcare settings, and you've given some examples of that at paragraph 28 of your
statement. What are the examples that you consider give rise to that appearance of
politicisation of those spaces?
DR GORDON: In terms of patients wearing - medical staff or healthcare staff
wearing uniforms at protests and online posting, is that what you are referring to?
MS PHILLIPS: They are the examples that you see as involving the politicisation
that you are seeking to -
DR GORDON: Correct. And as Jack spoke to, in the healthcare space specifically,
we are not looking to regulate private belief or prevent legitimate advocacy, but there
always needs to be consideration with what is being posted and the risk to the
patient. And we need a framework for what can be posted and what can't be posted.
COMMISSIONER: In your view, Doctor, if a medical practitioner identifies that he
or she comes from a particular institution, a particular public hospital, for example,
in a controversial social media post, that crosses a line?
DR GORDON: I think if it's visible to patients and they're taking a particular view
that - it all comes down to boundaries and what is being said. And that's where
a framework is needed, I think, to define exactly what can be said and what can't be
said. But I definitely think there are lines, and it's a matter of where those lines fall.
A patient needs to feel safe when they are seeking healthcare, as Jack mentioned, and
if a patient sees something that is posted by a doctor from the healthcare system and
the patient is interpreting is the healthcare system safe or not safe based on that post,
it needs to be not offensive to the patient.
And I think ultimately the patient is the centre of the system. The patient is
vulnerable. And as Jack mentioned, there is a power imbalance. The power lies with
the healthcare providers and the healthcare institutions. And we have a responsibility
with everything we do. As doctors, we take an oath to do what is in the best interests
of the patient. So there's this tension between, you know, what is in the best interests
of the patient and wanting to advocate for a political cause, and so we need to give
close consideration to that tension. But the top of the list should be patient welfare.

And if there's significant risk to the patient from - coming out of what has been
posted, in my mind, that's the priority.
COMMISSIONER: An area which has been controversial, I think, is where
a medical practitioner who has spent some time looking after patients in Gaza reports
his or her experiences on social media. In that circumstance, it only makes sense if
the person identifies that they are a medical practitioner, albeit it would not be
necessary for them to disclose where they are presently working. Do you have
a comment about that, Doctor?
DR GORDON: I don't find that in itself offensive. If they're looking to do good in
a particular community, in a particular part of the world, I think that's to be
commended. But it shouldn't veer into antisemitism. That's the point. So statements
about Jews or unfair statements about Israel that then reflect on Jews, I don't think
that's fair. But I think the fact they're going to do good in a part of the world is to be
commended.
COMMISSIONER: Yes, I think, Doctor, you wanted to come in on this, did you?
DR GREEN: I do, yes. Of course working in Gaza is - you know, there's no issue
with that. That's a good thing. Australians work in conflict zones all over the world.
And that's a good thing. But if you take that experience and you post it online as
a doctor and you connect that with false and misleading information or some sort of
selectively picked information or exaggerated information to push your political
view, now that might cross a line. So it really depends on what the post says.
MS PHILLIPS: Dr Gordon, you have commented in your statement - this is at
paragraph 24 - on having some engagement with medical insurers regarding updating
their educational material in relation to the safe use of social media and adherence to
social media guidelines. Can I ask you this, at a structural level, what role do medical
insurers or Medical Defence Organisations have to play in terms of promoting
particular standards of conduct amongst medical professionals, especially in those
spaces like the online environment?
DR GORDON: Yes. Well, we had discussions with AHPRA and with the Medical
Board, and we said to them, talk us through the process. If someone is reported, they
have a determination made against them by a National Board, the Medical Board,
what happens then? You make a direction and they need to be educated. Who does
the education? Who should we be speaking to, to make sure they receive the correct
education? Because often people are posting online very quickly. They're not
thinking about what they're posting; that's just human nature. And they don't realise
that what they are posting is offensive.
And so sometimes they're not meaning to do harm but it's an education issue. And I
think it's very important that they receive the correct education. So we were told by
AHPRA and the Medical Board that often the Medical Defence Organisations are
involved in that process and education of those people. And so we thought it was

important to approach the Medical Defence Organisations and just make sure what
education they were giving, and if we could help just to make sure they were giving
the correct education, firstly, to help the individual who has had a finding against
them so they understand what has happened so they don't fall into that trap again,
and also to protect the public who has sort of witnessed whatever has been posted or
happened.
MS PHILLIPS: And, Dr Gordon, can I take you to paragraph 12 of your witness
statement, and you have referred there to some of those engagements with AHPRA
that you have just mentioned, regarding the handling of antisemitism complaints and
the need for staff education. And you've also referred there to engaging with them
around the use of a standard accepted definition of antisemitism. Just putting to one
side for a moment what definition that might be - we will come to that in
a moment - why do you see the adoption of a definition of antisemitism as something
that has value in the context of complaints handling in the medical space?
DR GORDON: As I mentioned, our committee approached a number of regulators,
and we said to them, "This is happening. Help us understanding why it is
happening". And one of the issues that came out was that there wasn't a standard
definition being used, and that was creating difficulty and inconsistency in how cases
were being handled. So we said to AHPRA, being the national regulator, I think we
need consistency and we need a standard definition that's used to help the system, to
help healthcare practitioners and to help the public.
MS PHILLIPS: And, Dr Gordon, you have noted in your witness statement that
AHPRA has adopted the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance Working
Definition of Antisemitism, and you go on to make reference to the 15 National
Boards in Australia, and you express a concern in respect of the manner in which
those National Boards might conduct their adjudication functions. Can I ask you to
elaborate on that concern that you have identified?
DR GORDON: Sure. So we had communication with AHPRA at an early stage
about the use of a definition, and they adopted - or they didn't say they adopted but
they were using a standard definition from January of 2024, and that was the IHRA
definition. Even though it wasn't formally adopted at that point, they made it clear in
several emails that that is what they were doing and we thanked them for that.
But what was happening was people being reported, appropriately, because things
were inadvertently being posted that might be offensive, and the cases were seen by
AHPRA and deemed to be - need to come up for some kind of judgment. And the
people would come to whichever National Board, which is the body responsible for
making the adjudication, and then they would be dismissed from there and told
there'd been nothing wrong, and they would keep doing the same thing because, as
far as they were concerned, they had done nothing wrong because they'd been before
the National Board and told that they'd done nothing wrong, so not unreasonably
they kept doing the same thing, which unfortunately was the wrong thing to do
because of - it was offensive, and they'd be reported again, and there was this

revolving door situation where people were being reported, AHPRA said there was
a case to answer, the National Board would say they'd done nothing wrong, they'd be
dismissed, and then they'd be reported again and so on.
And so we tried to work out why that was happening. And why that was happening
was because the National Board is not under any obligation - or the National Boards
are not under any obligation to use the standard definitions that are provided to them
by AHPRA. So the way the system works is a case is reported to AHPRA. There will
be investigator at AHPRA who will put together the case. That includes standard
definitions. So in cases involving antisemitism, that will be the IHRA definition.
That is handed to the relevant National Board, and then the National Board is judge
and jury and makes a determination.
COMMISSIONER: The National Board, Doctor, is making a determination of
whether or not the doctor has breached his or her professional code of ethics; is that
broadly what the National Board is doing?
DR GORDON: Correct.
COMMISSIONER: So the National Board needs to be looking at the conduct of the
individual, including, presumably, consideration of the intent. One would not find
a doctor had engaged in antisemitic conduct if the doctor had not evinced a prejudice
or hostility against Jews, would one?
DR GORDON: Correct. But it comes to definition.
COMMISSIONER: This is the matter I'm taking up with you, Doctor.
DR GORDON: Okay. Yes.
COMMISSIONER: The definition is accompanied by examples.
DR GORDON: Correct.
COMMISSIONER: The examples are of occasions when expressive conduct might
evince a hatred of Jews.
DR GORDON: Correct.
COMMISSIONER: One can't isolate, in the context of disciplinary proceedings, an
example from a consideration of the conduct in its context.
DR GORDON: That's true. We did meet with the Medical Board to talk about this
issue, to try and work out what was going on and if there was indeed a gap. And so
because they're under no obligation to even consider the definitions that are provided
to them by AHPRA, and we couldn't discuss individual cases, so we didn't have
insight into exactly what was going on, we had concerns that the reason the cases

were falling through the gaps was because the IHRA definition wasn't being
considered.
So what we asked was, well, can you just make sure that the IHRA definition is
being considered and, as you say, if it's not antisemitic, then it's not antisemitic. But
we just want to make sure they're using the right framework. And the framework we
were asking them to use was the IHRA definition. So there's an inconsistency in that
AHPRA is using the IHRA definition, which is the framework, but the medical
boards aren't under any obligation to use the same framework, and because of that
inconsistency, we had this revolving door situation.
MS PHILLIPS: Dr Gordon, can I take you to a slightly different topic, which is
what you have said in your witness statement in connection with education,
particularly education concerning antisemitism. You pick up on this topic from
around paragraph 32 of your witness statement. Are you able to explain the way in
which you consider that antisemitism education could be embedded within existing
training programs or modules that doctors or medical trainees are required to
undertake?
DR GORDON: Yes. Well, at present, there's a requirement to do, in the workplace,
workplace health and safety training. And as part of that, there's cultural awareness
training. And I think antisemitism training is a natural fit into cultural awareness
training. So that's the case in the workplace and it's also the case in healthcare
professional training programs. So I think it's a natural fit in both those situations.
MS PHILLIPS: And, Dr Gordon, is it right that your patient cohort in your own
practice includes a number of Jewish patients?
DR GORDON: Correct.
MS PHILLIPS: And are you able to outline any concerns that your patients have
raised with you in the last couple of years around accessing healthcare or medical
procedures in your practice?
DR GORDON: I have quite a large Jewish patient population, and on a regular basis
I have patients expressing concern about - I'm a gastroenterologist. I do procedures in
hospital. And people ask me, "Am I safe going to that hospital?" and patients are in
a very vulnerable situation, and particularly patients who are having procedures,
they're essentially unconscious. You know, they are under an anaesthetic. And they
are worried about what is going to happen to them. Firstly, are they going to be
exposed to antisemitic sentiment when they go to this place, and, secondly, am
I going to be taken care of and what's going to happen to me when I am
unconscious?
MS PHILLIPS: And are you able to isolate the time period in which these sorts of
concerns first started escalating, insofar as they were taken up with you by your
patients?

DR GORDON: I have never been asked a question along those lines before October
7, 2023 and I've been in private practice since 2006.
MS PHILLIPS: And at paragraph 35 of your witness statement, you've said that
given the loss of trust in the sense of safety amongst the Jewish community that
you've earlier described, you consider that public healthcare services need to make
visible commitments to the safety of Jewish patients and staff. What are some of the
visible commitments that you have in mind there?
DR GORDON: Well, I think, firstly, the main visible commitment is removing
political advocacy from healthcare, because that's a sign we're taking a stand. It's
what's being done in Victoria, and I think it should be done nationally. Healthcare,
again, is about the patient. The patient is the focus. The patient is vulnerable.
Everything we do, we need to consider how is this going to impact the patient and
only do what is in the best interests of the patient. To do otherwise, there's this
additional burden of a concern on the part of the patient, where do I fit into this new
entity, political advocacy? If I'm on the wrong side of the political advocacy, am
I going to be treated fairly?
And it's not just an issue relating to the Jewish community. I speak to patients from
other minority ethnic communities and also doctors from other ethnic minority
communities. And they are of the same view. Everyone wants the healthcare system
to be safe and equitable for everybody, and there shouldn't be this additional concern
placed on patients about where they fit in terms of the political advocacy of the day.
Healthcare should be a sacred space.
MS PHILLIPS: Dr Green, can I return to you. Paragraph 68 of your witness
statement, you've outlined the healthcare environment that you hope to see. What
does that include, for your part?
DR GREEN: I might read. So:
"Antisemitism within healthcare is not an isolated or episodic concern. It is
a systemic challenge affecting professional conduct, workplace culture, patient trust
and the ethical integrity of healthcare. The healthcare environment that I hope to see
is one in which clinical settings remain focused on patient care, professionalism,
impartiality and respect, no practitioner feels compelled to conceal their Jewish or
Israeli identity, no patient doubts their care will be impartial, no colleague is
collectively blamed for the actions of a foreign government, and no minority group is
made to feel that it might be treated different to other patients.
Achieving that environment requires more than statements of principle. It must
clearly identify unacceptable conduct; establish and consistently enforce
professional standards; provide robust, fair and accessible complaints processes;
monitor compliance; and impose meaningful consequences where those standards
are breached.

This must be supported by education, clear professional boundaries and leadership
that treats antisemitism as seriously as other forms of racism and identity-based
discrimination."
And the last point is:
"I think a better future is possible. Protecting Jewish healthcare workers and
patients from antisemitism will also preserve the trust on which healthcare depends,
uphold the ethical integrity of medicine and contribute to the social cohesion that
this Royal Commission was established to strengthen."
